title: Gastrointestinal Histology
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter teaches the microscopic structure of the digestive tube and its glands: the four-layer wall and its nerve plexuses, the epithelium of each region, the cells of the gastric gland, the features that identify each intestinal segment, the liver lobule and acinus, and the exocrine pancreas and salivary glands. Board questions usually show a section or describe a cell and ask what it makes, where it sits, or what fails when it is lost. Each structure here is explained by its job, so that a finding such as high gastrin with low acid, or necrosis around the central vein, can be reasoned out rather than memorized.
prerequisites: Basic tissue types: epithelium, connective tissue, smooth and skeletal muscle
Cell organelles and the secretory pathway (rough endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi, secretory granules)
Gross anatomy of the digestive tract, peritoneum, and retroperitoneum (GI-1)
Germ layers and derivatives of the foregut, midgut, and hindgut
Hematoxylin and eosin staining: what basophilia and eosinophilia indicate

connections.how: The cells and plexuses identified here are the effectors of gastric acid secretion, enzyme release, and peristalsis.
Intrinsic factor from parietal cells and cytochrome P450 in zone 3 hepatocytes link gastric and liver histology to B12 deficiency and toxic metabolites.
Lamina propria lymphocytes, Peyer patches, and M cells form the gut-associated lymphoid tissue that samples antigen and drives IgA responses.

connections.to: Pathology of the esophagus, stomach, and liver
connections.how: Barrett metaplasia, autoimmune gastritis, and zonal hepatic necrosis are explained directly by the histology of each organ.
Neural crest migration forms the enteric plexuses, and the endoderm and ectoderm junction at the pectinate line sets the anal canal's epithelium and drainage.

terms.def: The thin layer of smooth muscle that forms the deepest part of the mucosa and separates it from the submucosa.
The intrinsic neurons of the gut wall, organized as the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses, that can run secretion and motility without input from the brain.
Pacemaker cells associated with the myenteric plexus that generate the slow waves of gut smooth muscle.
Reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another that better withstands a chronic stress.
The line in the anal canal where hindgut endoderm meets the ectoderm of the proctodeum, marking a change in epithelium, blood supply, lymph drainage, and nerves.
The acid-secreting gland of the gastric fundus and body, containing parietal, chief, mucous neck, enterochromaffin-like, and D cells.
A glycoprotein from parietal cells that binds vitamin B12 and is required for its uptake in the terminal ileum.
Submucosal glands of the duodenum that secrete alkaline mucus to protect the mucosa from gastric acid.
A specialized epithelial cell over Peyer patches that transports luminal antigens and microbes to underlying immune cells.
The narrow space between the sinusoidal endothelium and hepatocytes, into which hepatocyte microvilli project and where stellate cells live.
The functional unit of the liver, centered on the terminal branches of a portal triad and divided into zones 1 to 3 by distance from that blood supply.
A pale duct cell, unique to the pancreas, that lies inside the acinus where the intercalated duct begins.

sections.title: The four layers of the gut wall and the enteric plexuses

blocks.text: From the esophagus to the anal canal, the digestive tube is built on one plan of four concentric layers. Learning that plan once lets you read any section: identify the layers first, then look for the local changes in epithelium, glands, folds, and lymphoid tissue that identify the segment (C02 and C04).

The mucosa has three parts. The epithelium protects, secretes, and absorbs. The lamina propria beneath it is loose connective tissue with capillaries, lymphatics (the lacteals of the small intestine), and many lymphocytes and plasma cells, which makes the mucosa a major immune organ. The muscularis mucosae, a thin sheet of smooth muscle, moves the mucosa independently of the wall and marks the mucosa's lower border. That border matters in the colon, where the lamina propria has few lymphatics: a carcinoma confined above the muscularis mucosae rarely spreads, while one that crosses it into the submucosa can reach lymphatics and metastasize.

The submucosa is dense connective tissue carrying larger vessels and lymphatics, glands in the esophagus and duodenum, and the submucosal (Meissner) plexus. The muscularis externa has an inner circular layer that narrows the lumen and an outer longitudinal layer that shortens the segment; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus lies between them and coordinates the two into peristalsis, with interstitial cells of Cajal setting the slow-wave rhythm. Each plexus sits beside what it controls: the submucosal plexus regulates glandular secretion, mucosal blood flow, and the muscularis mucosae, and the myenteric plexus regulates motility.

blocks.title: Layers of the gut wall
rows: Epithelium changes by region; villi only in the small intestine
Dense connective tissue, vessels, lymphatics, Meissner plexus
Glands in the esophagus and duodenum (Brunner); Peyer patches extend into it in the ileum
Inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle, Auerbach plexus between them
Stomach adds an inner oblique layer; upper esophagus is skeletal muscle; colon gathers longitudinal muscle into taeniae coli
Serosa: mesothelium on connective tissue. Adventitia: connective tissue only
Serosa over intraperitoneal organs; adventitia over the thoracic esophagus and the nonperitoneal surfaces of retroperitoneal segments
blocks.caption: The circular layer thickens locally to form sphincters such as the pylorus and the internal anal sphincter.

blocks.text: The outer coat depends on the peritoneum. Organs suspended in the peritoneal cavity are covered by serosa, a mesothelium that lets them slide. Where peritoneum is absent, as around the thoracic esophagus and behind retroperitoneal segments such as most of the duodenum and the ascending and descending colon, adventitia anchors the organ instead. With no serosal barrier, esophageal cancer spreads readily into the mediastinum.

Enteric neurons derive from neural crest cells that migrate down the gut from cranial to caudal. Inhibitory motor neurons, which release nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide, are needed for smooth muscle to relax, so losing them causes failure of relaxation rather than paralysis. In achalasia, loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons keeps the lower esophageal sphincter closed; Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease) destroys the plexus with similar effects.

blocks.title: Hirschsprung disease from missing ganglion cells
steps: Neural crest cells fail to complete migration
Distal colon lacks ganglion cells in both plexuses
No inhibitory neurons, so the segment cannot relax
Tonically contracted segment causes functional obstruction
Bowel above dilates (megacolon); meconium passage is delayed
blocks.caption: The aganglionic segment always begins at the rectum and extends proximally for a variable length.

blocks.predict: A rectal suction biopsy samples only mucosa and submucosa. How can it diagnose Hirschsprung disease when the myenteric plexus lies deeper?
blocks.explain: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus lies in the submucosa, and in Hirschsprung disease both plexuses lack ganglion cells. Absent submucosal ganglion cells, usually with hypertrophied nerve trunks, are enough.
blocks.check: The location of each plexus in the layer table.

sections.title: Epithelium along the tube and Barrett metaplasia

blocks.text: The epithelium in each region matches its main stress. Where food or stool rubs the surface, many cell layers protect it and are shed and replaced from below. Where the job is secretion or absorption, a single layer of columnar cells keeps the distance to blood short.

blocks.title: Epithelium by region
rows: Resists abrasion from swallowed food; submucosal glands lubricate
Simple columnar; every surface cell secretes mucus (no goblet cells)
Mucus and bicarbonate gel protect against acid
Simple columnar enterocytes with brush border, plus goblet cells
Simple columnar in straight crypts, many goblet cells
Water and salt absorption; mucus lubricates drying stool
Simple columnar (colorectal type), then a narrow transitional zone
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous, becoming keratinized skin at the anal verge
blocks.caption: Abrupt junctions occur at the gastroesophageal junction and the pectinate line.

blocks.text: At the gastroesophageal junction the pale squamous mucosa meets the red columnar gastric mucosa at an irregular squamocolumnar junction (Z line). Reflux of acid, pepsin, and bile bathes the squamous side, which lacks the surface mucus and bicarbonate layer that protects the stomach. With chronic injury the distal esophagus can undergo metaplasia: the squamous lining is replaced by columnar epithelium of intestinal type, which resists acid better. Endoscopically, salmon-colored tongues of mucosa extend upward from the junction.

Barrett esophagus is diagnosed on biopsy by intestinal metaplasia: columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. Goblet cells are the key, because normal esophageal and gastric surface epithelium contains none. Metaplasia protects in the short term, but the cells continue to divide under inflammatory stress and accumulate mutations (TP53 loss is common), so the lining can progress through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma of the distal esophagus. Squamous cell carcinoma, by contrast, arises from squamous epithelium, usually in the middle third, and is linked to tobacco and alcohol.

blocks.title: From reflux to esophageal adenocarcinoma
steps: Chronic reflux of acid, pepsin, and bile
Repeated injury to distal squamous epithelium
Intestinal metaplasia: columnar cells with goblet cells
Accumulating mutations produce dysplasia
Invasive adenocarcinoma of the distal esophagus
blocks.caption: Each step is a histologic stage that a biopsy can identify.

blocks.text: The pectinate line marks where the endoderm of the hindgut meets the ectoderm of the proctodeum. Because two embryologic territories meet there, the epithelium, vessels, lymphatics, and nerves all change at the same line, and the table below lets you predict the behavior of hemorrhoids and cancers on either side.

blocks.title: Above versus below the pectinate line
rows: Superior rectal to the portal system
Inferior rectal to the systemic (caval) system
Internal iliac and inferior mesenteric nodes
Somatic (inferior rectal branch of pudendal); painful
Squamous cell carcinoma, often HPV related
blocks.caption: The portal and systemic venous connection here is a site of portosystemic anastomosis.

sections.title: Gastric gland cells and autoimmune gastritis

blocks.text: The stomach has three glandular regions. The cardia and the antrum (pyloric region) have mainly mucous glands, and the antral glands also contain G cells. The fundus and body have oxyntic glands, which make acid and enzymes. An oxyntic gland opens into a gastric pit lined by surface mucous cells; below it lie the isthmus, which holds the stem cells, then the neck with mucous neck cells and many parietal cells, then the base with chief cells.

blocks.title: Cells of the gastric glands
rows: Fundus and body, mostly upper half of gland
Large, round, central nucleus, pink cytoplasm (fried egg)
blocks.caption: Parietal and chief cells are confined to the fundus and body; G cells are in the antrum.

blocks.text: Appearance follows function. Parietal cells are pink because they are packed with mitochondria that supply ATP to the H+/K+-ATPase. At rest the pump is stored in tubulovesicles; on stimulation by acetylcholine, gastrin, and histamine these fuse with deep intracellular canaliculi, multiplying the secretory surface. Carbonic anhydrase supplies H+, and the matching bicarbonate exits into blood in exchange for Cl-, producing the postprandial alkaline tide. Chief cells are basophilic because of rough endoplasmic reticulum making pepsinogen, which acid converts to pepsin.

blocks.title: Acid feedback on gastrin
steps: Meal buffers acid; antral pH rises
G cells release gastrin into blood
Gastrin stimulates ECL histamine and parietal acid
Antral pH falls
D cells release somatostatin
Somatostatin suppresses G cells; gastrin falls
blocks.caption: Acid in the antrum is the main brake on gastrin. Removing acid removes the brake.

blocks.text: Autoimmune gastritis is directed at the oxyntic mucosa. CD4 T cells attack the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase, and antibodies to parietal cells and intrinsic factor appear. Fundic and body glands atrophy and are partly replaced by intestinal metaplasia, while the antrum, which has no parietal cells, is spared. This distribution distinguishes it from Helicobacter pylori gastritis, which usually begins in the antrum.

blocks.title: Predicted secretions in autoimmune gastritis
rows: Made by chief and mucous neck cells of oxyntic glands
Antral G cells intact; no acid to trigger somatostatin
Gastrin is trophic to ECL cells; hyperplasia can form neuroendocrine tumors
blocks.caption: Every loss is a body and fundus product; every rise comes from the spared antrum or from gastrin acting downstream.

blocks.text: Loss of intrinsic factor prevents B12 uptake in the terminal ileum. Because the liver stores several years of B12, pernicious anemia appears late, with megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts. Achlorhydria also reduces nonheme iron absorption and raises the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

blocks.title: Reading the laboratory pattern
blocks.text: A woman with hypothyroidism has fatigue, macrocytic anemia, and reduced vibration sense. Serum gastrin is very high and pepsinogen I is low. First, high gastrin has two possible sources: a gastrinoma, or loss of acid feedback. Low pepsinogen I says chief cells of the oxyntic mucosa are gone, which favors atrophy rather than a tumor; a gastrinoma would bring high acid and ulcers, not atrophy. Atrophy of the body and fundus also removes parietal cells, explaining achlorhydria and lost intrinsic factor, which explains B12 deficiency, macrocytosis, and dorsal column signs. Coexisting autoimmune thyroid disease fits autoimmune gastritis.

sections.title: Identifying the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and colon

blocks.text: The small intestine enlarges its absorptive surface at three scales. Plicae circulares are permanent folds of mucosa with a submucosal core; villi are finger-like projections of mucosa, each with a capillary network and a central lacteal; and microvilli form the brush border of each enterocyte. Together they expand the surface several hundredfold compared with a flat tube. Between the villi, tubular crypts (of Lieberkuhn) extend down to the muscularis mucosae. Stem cells near the crypt base renew the epithelium every few days, and Paneth cells at the very base, with bright eosinophilic granules, release lysozyme and defensins that shape the crypt's microbial environment.

The segments share this plan, so they are told apart by a few added features, each explained by the segment's job. The duodenum receives acidic chyme from the stomach, so Brunner glands in its submucosa secrete alkaline mucus to protect the mucosa until pancreatic bicarbonate arrives. The jejunum does most nutrient absorption, so it has the tallest and most closely spaced plicae and long villi. The ileum faces a larger bacterial load and carries Peyer patches: aggregated lymphoid follicles in the lamina propria that bulge into the submucosa, on the side opposite the mesentery. The epithelium over them contains M cells, which pass antigens to dendritic cells and lymphocytes and start IgA responses. The terminal ileum also absorbs the B12 and intrinsic factor complex and reabsorbs bile acids.

The colon absorbs water and salt and lubricates stool, so it has no villi and no plicae circulares, only straight crypts crowded with goblet cells. Its outer longitudinal muscle is gathered into three taeniae coli, which pucker the wall into haustra.

blocks.title: Distinguishing features of each segment
rows: Normally absent beyond the proximal colon
blocks.caption: Villi separate small intestine from colon; Brunner glands mark the duodenum; Peyer patches mark the ileum.

blocks.title: Naming a segment from a section
blocks.text: A slide shows simple columnar epithelium with tall villi and crypts. Large lymphoid follicles with germinal centers fill the lamina propria and push into the submucosa, and the submucosa contains no glands. Work in order. Villi are present, so this is small intestine, not colon or appendix. No submucosal glands rules out the duodenum. Organized lymphoid follicles extending into the submucosa are Peyer patches, so the segment is ileum. If the same section had tall closely packed plicae without large follicles, it would be jejunum. A small lymphoid aggregate alone does not prove ileum, because solitary follicles occur throughout the gut.

These features predict where disease appears. Celiac disease injures the proximal small bowel, where gluten arrives first, flattening villi and lengthening crypts; iron and folate, absorbed proximally, become deficient. Salmonella Typhi and Yersinia enter through M cells, so typhoid ulcers form over Peyer patches and can perforate. Crohn disease favors the terminal ileum, causing B12 deficiency and bile acid loss. Paneth cells appearing in the distal colon signal chronic mucosal injury, as in ulcerative colitis.

sections.title: The hepatic lobule, acinus, and zonal injury

blocks.text: Hepatocytes form plates one to two cells thick separated by sinusoids. The liver receives about 75% of its blood from the portal vein, carrying absorbed nutrients and toxins, and about 25% from the hepatic artery, which is richer in oxygen. Branches of both, with a bile duct and lymphatics, run together in each portal triad (portal tract). Blood from both mixes in the sinusoids, flows toward the central vein, and leaves through the hepatic veins. Bile moves in the opposite direction, from canaliculi between hepatocytes toward the bile duct in the triad.

The same tissue can be divided in two useful ways. The classic lobule is a hexagon centered on a central vein with portal triads at its corners; it is easy to see on a slide. The acinus is centered instead on the terminal vessels running between two triads and extends to the two nearest central veins. Because it follows the direction of blood flow, the acinus explains injury patterns.

The sinusoidal endothelium has open fenestrations and almost no basement membrane, so plasma, including large proteins and lipoproteins, passes freely into the space of Disse, where hepatocyte microvilli exchange material with it. Two other cell types live at this interface.

blocks.title: Cells and spaces of the sinusoid
rows: Loses fenestrations and gains a basement membrane in cirrhosis
Filled with collagen in fibrosis, impairing exchange
Macrophages clearing gut bacteria, debris, old red cells
Release cytokines that activate stellate cells
Store vitamin A in lipid droplets
Become myofibroblasts that lay down collagen
blocks.caption: In chronic injury, TGF-beta and other signals turn quiescent stellate cells into collagen-producing myofibroblasts, the central event in fibrosis and cirrhosis.

blocks.text: Zone 1 hepatocytes lie next to the triad and receive blood first, so they get the most oxygen and nutrients; they are rich in enzymes of gluconeogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and urea synthesis. Zone 3 hepatocytes surround the central vein and receive blood last, after upstream cells have extracted much of the oxygen, so their oxygen tension is lowest. Zone 3 also contains the most cytochrome P450, including CYP2E1. Both facts make zone 3 the most vulnerable to hypoperfusion and to drugs that become toxic when metabolized. Shock causes centrilobular necrosis, right heart failure causes centrilobular congestion (nutmeg liver), and alcohol injury is also concentrated there. Zone 1 meets portal blood first, and periportal necrosis is typical of eclampsia; zone 2 necrosis is classic for yellow fever.

blocks.title: Acetaminophen injury in zone 3
steps: Overdose saturates glucuronidation and sulfation
CYP2E1 oxidizes excess drug to reactive NAPQI
Zone 3 glutathione is depleted
NAPQI binds proteins, damaging mitochondria
Centrilobular (zone 3) hepatocyte necrosis
blocks.caption: Injury is greatest where the oxidizing enzyme is most concentrated and glutathione is first exhausted.

blocks.predict: Why does a chronic heavy drinker develop liver injury after a smaller acetaminophen overdose than a nondrinker?
blocks.explain: Chronic alcohol use induces CYP2E1, so more NAPQI forms, and poor nutrition lowers glutathione stores, so less is neutralized. Both changes act in zone 3.
blocks.check: The zone 3 enzyme content and the acetaminophen flow.

sections.title: Exocrine pancreas, islets, and salivary glands

blocks.text: The pancreas and the salivary glands are both branched glands whose secretory acini drain through a tree of ducts. An acinus makes the protein product; the ducts modify the water and electrolytes.

The pancreatic acinar cell is a classic protein-exporting cell. Its base is deeply basophilic from rough endoplasmic reticulum, and its apex is filled with eosinophilic zymogen granules. These store inactive proenzymes (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase) with amylase and lipase, plus a trypsin inhibitor that protects the cell. Pale centroacinar cells sit inside the acinus where the intercalated duct begins; with the duct cells they secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid through CFTR in response to secretin, flushing the enzymes to the duodenum. Premature activation of trypsin inside acinar cells causes autodigestion in acute pancreatitis.

Islets of Langerhans are pale, rounded clusters scattered among the acini, making up only about 1% to 2% of pancreatic mass. They look pale because endocrine cells lack the dense rough endoplasmic reticulum and large zymogen granules of acinar cells. They have no ducts and secrete into a rich network of fenestrated capillaries: beta cells (insulin) are the majority, with alpha (glucagon), delta (somatostatin), and PP cells. Because islets and acini are separate, disease can remove one and spare the other. In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR leaves secretions thick, ducts plug, and acini atrophy and fibrose, while islets persist until late, when diabetes may develop.

Salivary acini come in two types. Serous cells have round basal nuclei, basophilic cytoplasm, and granules of watery, protein-rich secretion containing amylase, so serous acini stain dark. Mucous cells look pale and foamy, with nuclei flattened against the base, because the mucin they store is lost during tissue processing. In mixed glands, serous cells can cap mucous tubules as serous demilunes. Myoepithelial cells around the acini contract to expel saliva. Striated ducts, lined by cells with basal infoldings and many mitochondria, reabsorb Na+ and Cl- and secrete K+ and bicarbonate, which makes saliva hypotonic.

blocks.title: Telling the salivary glands and pancreas apart
rows: Striated ducts; adipocytes increase with age; no islets
Islets and centroacinar cells; no striated ducts
blocks.caption: Parotid and pancreas both look purely serous, so islets and centroacinar cells identify the pancreas.

blocks.text: Shared histology explains shared disease. Mumps virus targets serous glands, causing parotitis and sometimes pancreatitis, and either can raise serum amylase. In Sjogren syndrome, lymphocytes destroy salivary and lacrimal acini, producing dry mouth and eyes.

integration.text: Embryology and anatomy set the structure: neural crest migration builds the enteric plexuses, and the meeting of endoderm and ectoderm sets the anal canal's pectinate line. The peritoneal relationship of each segment decides whether it carries serosa or adventitia and therefore how a tumor spreads.

Physiology, biochemistry, immunology, and pathology then follow from the cells. Parietal cells link the stomach to B12 metabolism and autoimmunity; the gastrin and somatostatin loop explains why atrophy raises gastrin; M cells and Peyer patches link the ileum to mucosal immunity and to enteric infection; and the oxygen and enzyme gradient across the acinus explains zonal necrosis. Section features overlap, so a single lymphoid aggregate or a few goblet cells can mislead; identify a section from several features together.

summary: The gut wall has mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa or adventitia; the Meissner plexus in the submucosa controls secretion and blood flow, and the Auerbach plexus between the muscle layers controls motility.
Hirschsprung disease is absence of ganglion cells in both plexuses from failed neural crest migration, so the distal segment cannot relax.
Stratified squamous epithelium lines the esophagus and the anal canal below the pectinate line; simple columnar epithelium lines the stomach through the upper anal canal.
Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells caused by chronic reflux and is the precursor of distal esophageal adenocarcinoma.
Parietal cells (HCl, intrinsic factor) and chief cells (pepsinogen) are in the fundus and body; G cells (gastrin) are in the antrum.
Autoimmune gastritis destroys body and fundus glands: acid, intrinsic factor, and pepsinogen I fall, gastrin rises from the spared antrum, and B12 deficiency follows.
Villi mean small intestine; Brunner glands mean duodenum, tall plicae mean jejunum, Peyer patches mean ileum, and goblet-rich crypts without villi mean colon.
Blood flows from portal triad to central vein, so zone 3 has the least oxygen and the most CYP2E1 and is injured first by ischemia and acetaminophen.
Kupffer cells are sinusoidal macrophages; stellate cells in the space of Disse store vitamin A and become collagen-producing myofibroblasts in fibrosis.
Pancreatic acini have basophilic bases and zymogen granules; pale islets and centroacinar cells distinguish the pancreas from the purely serous parotid.

verify: Hepatic blood supply is quoted as about 75% portal and 25% arterial by volume; oxygen delivery is often quoted as about half from each source, and figures vary between texts.

Barrett esophagus is defined by goblet cell intestinal metaplasia in United States guidelines, while some other guidelines accept columnar metaplasia without goblet cells; confirm the definition NABNE uses.
The fraction of pancreatic mass made of islets (about 1% to 2%) and the proportions of islet cell types vary by source and species.
Zonal associations beyond zone 3 (periportal necrosis in eclampsia, midzonal necrosis in yellow fever) are classic teaching associations; confirm which NABNE expects.
The statement that plicae circulares begin beyond the first part of the duodenum and are absent in the distal ileum reflects standard histology texts; exact limits vary.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I uses the eponyms Meissner, Auerbach, Brunner, Lieberkuhn, Disse, Ito, and Kupffer or the descriptive names.
